newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. officials due in Brussels for Boeing talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials due in Brussels for Boeing talks.

text.p: U.S. Justice Department officials are due in Brussels by Saturday for talks with anti-trust counterparts in the European Commission on the planned Boeing/McDonnell Douglas merger.

The unusual weekend meeting takes place less than two weeks before the European Union executive is due to vote on whether to approve the $14 billion merger to create the world's largest aerospace company.
EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has made clear the deal could not be approved without Boeing offering "structural" changes to address EU anti-trust concerns.

However, both U.S. and EU officials said the consultations between top Justice Department anti-trust official Joel Klein and EU competition officials would focus on a U.S./EU competition policy agreement, and would not involve negotiating changes to allow the merger to proceed.
An EU source said it had nothing to do "with whatever discussions might take place" between Boeing and the Commission's competition officials on possible remedies.
"If Mr Joel Klein is around, it is not, I repeat, it is not to 'negotiate' or discuss the Boeing merger case with European Commission officials," the EU source said.
Instead, they would discuss how the cooperation between EU and U.S. competition authorities had functioned and how it could be improved.
A U.S. official told Reuters early on Friday that Klein would be in Brussels with other aides by "this time tomorrow".
Klein's visit was "an opportunity for us to explain why we did what with the Federal Trade Commission" on Boeing.

"Since the FTC has blessed this thing, obviously the view of the U.S. government is that the deal should go through. If the EU were not to agree on that, it does not take a genius to figure out what's going to happen then," the official added.

The FTC cleared the deal with no conditions last week, saying McDonnell's commercial aircraft activity was no longer a viable stand-alone business while dropping a heavy hint that it could live with some EU action against Boeing's exclusive aircraft supply deals to several airlines.

Commission thinking, backed last Friday by anti-trust officials from EU national capitals, is that McDonnell's assets are nevertheless valuable to a merged company and that Boeing should offer some remedy in return for EU approval.

Next Monday is the "drop-dead date" for doing a deal between EU competition officials and the two merging companies, the U.S. official said, meaning that after that day, the Commission will be hard-pushed to complete its preparations for its scheduled decision on July 23.
